The Smart Manufacturing Delivery RET (RoviSys Execution Template) is our project delivery flow based on our Dx procedures.  T his 
template outlines how each of the procedures flow together to define how we execute a comprehensive project within our "Agile for 
Manufacturing" mindset.  This mindset enables the continuous refinement of project scope throughout the lifecycle of a 
digitalization initiative. It bridges the gaps between purely agile and purely waterfall execution methodologies, addressing key 
challenges of both approaches.
Challenges with pure agile execution:
Lack of overall project goals and clear scope boundaries○
Absence of a comprehensive roadmap, leading to an unclear definition of completion○
Increased risk of cost overruns and unmet customer expectations○•
Challenges with pure waterfall execution:
Rigid scope boundaries that limit flexibility and course correction○
Heavy reliance on upfront functional and design requirements, which can be impractical○
Risk of weak or incomplete design deliverables that may not be fully understood by the customer at the time of review○•
By leveraging the strengths of both methodologies with that "Agile for Manufacturing" mindset, our Smart Manufacturing delive ry 
flow provides a more adaptable, goal -oriented approach that drives project success and enhances customer satisfaction.
The RoviSys Smart Manufacturing Delivery brings together the key components from our suite of Dx procedures, all designed to 
drive a successful digitalization initiative. The package is organized into three core phases: Assessment, Execution, and Dep loyment. 
Throughout each phase, we continuously refine the scope -transforming high -level objectives into detailed, actionable technical 
tasks. Below is a description of each phase:

designed as a short, lightweight engagement that:
Establishes the current process state•
Defines the rationale behind the digitalization initiative•
Identifies how digitalization will enhance operations•
Develops a strategy to quantify costs and measure success•

The assessment is meant to be a relatively lightweight engagement that establishes the current process 
state, the rationale behind the digitalization initiative, the manner in which digitalization will be 
leveraged to provide positive impact to operations, and a strategy for quantifying the success of the 
initiative.  Additionally, the assessment identifies the digitalization tools (platforms, technologies, etc.) 
that will be leveraged, as well as an overall deployment roadmap for these technologies.  The 
assessment commonly serves as an 'entry point' for RoviSys when working with a customer who is 
interested in an MES.  It is difficult if not impossible to accurately estimate the overall scope of the 
initiative until the assessment has been completed.  However, it is possible that the customer has 
already completed initial work that can be leveraged to shorten the assessment effort.  
The following chart details the sequence of events (features) typically executed as part of a holistic 
assessment effort.  Note that some features irrelevant to a holistic digitalization effort have been 
omitted.  These features may be required if the DxDiscovery product is being executed by itself, and/or 
in the case of a more control systems / automation -centric assessment.

The ultimate goal of the DxDiscovery product offering is to gather information that will shape the 
remainder of the engagement.  This includes a recommendation concerning the path forward, which 
may include execution of the DxArchitecture and/or DxLean productized services offerings.  
The discovery effort does not provide a detailed roadmap, design for the solution, or allow for the build 
and deployment of any software component.  These expectations must be managed with the customer.  
The following is a breakdown of the general activities conducted as part of the DxDiscovery effort.  The 
execution of each process is further described in corresponding RIS documents.  
Discovery Quotation:
The customer must be given a proposal for the discovery effort.  This proposal should clarify the 
duration of the effort, execution strategy, required meetings, deliverables, and associated costs.  
RACI Formulation:
RACI formulation aids in the definition of the various participants in the effort, and their responsibilities, 
both from RoviSys and customer perspectives.  This includes not just the project team itself, but also 
various stakeholders who will need to participate in current process state explanations, interviews, and 
deliverable review.  
Infrastructure Evaluation:
An evaluation of the infrastructure in place across the enterprise is often required to evaluate its ability 
to support a digitalization initiative, identifying aspects that may need to be bolstered as part of the 
effort.  Infrastructure includes both process control and enterprise plan networks, cloud connectivity, 
provisioned cloud infrastructure, integration layers and associated integration applications in place 
(such as OPC servers, MQTT brokers, etc.), cybersecurity resilience, and data analytics layers (data 
warehouses, data lakes, etc.).  
Legacy System Review:
Often a manufacturing enterprise is already leveraging legacy systems / applications as part of their 
existing digitalization footprint.  It is important that these legacy applications are properly understood, 
including the role of each, functionality provided, and any issues -including both useability and 
maintenance concerns.  This will help to ensure no key piece of legacy functionality is overlooked and 
that ultimately a holistic architecture is created detailing which applications will be replaced and which 
will be integrated into the future solution.  
Site Walk Evaluation:
A site walkdown includes a tour of the facility, showing the RoviSys team how product flows, how 
individuals interact with the process, and the environment in which individuals perform their daily work.  
This provides a first -hand view of the manufacturing process, including identification of physical and 
logistical constraints and opportunities that can be factored into the recommended path forward.  A site 
walk also provides an opportunity to ask questions directly to shop -floor personnel that can give 
valuable perspective not able to be obtained from other customer stakeholders.  This activity enables 
consideration of the sizing of the facility into future quotation efforts.  Potential interaction points and 
associated devices, such as tablets, terminals, scanners, readers, etc. can be envisioned and the MES RAP 101 -DxDiscovery

Panel Walk Down:
This feature consists of inventorying, assessing, and inspecting the control system panels within the 
facility to determine their location, serviced machinery, and hardware age, as well as to evaluate the 
layout, organization, and clarity of wiring and component identification in each cabinet.  This enables 
RoviSys to recommend improvements to the control system infrastructure, including hardware 
upgrades or improved organization.  Such improvements can be properly phased, leading to 
minimal production impact.  
Legacy Documentation Review:
A review of any legacy documentation possessed by the enterprise, including legacy system design 
documents, user guides, training guides, process flow diagrams, etc. can help give RoviSys a better 
understanding of the legacy systems and processes in place within the facility.  This allows RoviSys to ask 
more thoughtful, relevant questions during other DxDiscovery activities such as site walks and 
stakeholder interviews rather than spend time asking high -level questions simply to obtain sufficient 
background.  
Operations Management Capability Review:
In many cases, a customer may be unfamiliar with the capabilities provided by an MES or MOM 
application, and there may be confusion as to the scope of the initiative as a result.  Even customers 
familiar with the digitalization of operations management functions may lack a deep understanding of 
capabilities provided by the different layers in the ISA -95 model, considering such systems as ERP, 
MES/MOM, SCADA, etc.  During this activity, RoviSys provides an overview of the capabilities provided 
as part of a digitalized ISA -95 compliant solution stack, focusing particularly on Level 3 capabilities most 
often provided by Layer 3 applications.  
Current Process State Definition:
This effort helps to baseline the current state of the facility or facilities under the scope of the 
assessment.  This exercise gives RoviSys background concerning current shop floor activities and system -
level processes that will help to frame the rest of the assessment effort.  
Stakeholder Group Interview Process:
During this activity, RoviSys learns more from key personnel in the enterprise about the processes and 
activities observed during current state process definition.  Probing questions are asked that allows 
RoviSys to draw conclusions concerning what processes work well and what processes could be 
enhanced by a greater degree of digitalization.  
Perceived Benefit: (Next Steps Value Identification)
During this activity, the perceived benefit of pursuing a next step is documented and a justification 
formulated.  While a formal ROI analysis is not typically conducted at this stage, distillment of the 
benefits of moving forward will aid the customer in justifying a larger initiative and provide the customer 
a more specific focus for constrained budgets and resources.  For example, RoviSys may recommend a 
DxArchitecture engagement, DxLean engagement, pilot DxExecution project, or a combination of all 
these productized services offerings.

The RASCI model specifies definition of stakeholders as follows:
Responsible for ensuring completion of the activity.  The responsible person is the one who does 
the work to complete the task or create the deliverable.  Typically, a RoviSys resource is named as 
responsible for the completion of the various Assessment deliverables, although the customer 
may be responsible for providing prerequisite information.  -
Accountable for reviewing and confirming the completion of the activity.  The accountable party 
approves the deliverable provided as a result of a given assessment activity.  
Typically, a customer resource is named as the accountable party, ensuring the provided 
deliverable is accurate and soliciting feedback from other consulted parties.  Rather than 
requiring the document be signed off by many reviewers, one accountable party helped to 
streamline review and approval cycles.  ○

These individuals are typically customer roles who need to be kept abreast of the progress of the 
activity by being provided status updates, or being included in status update meetings.  They 
might include heads or directors of affected customer teams and senior customer leadership.-
The RoviSys templatized assessment agenda and RACI/RASCI template will both contain generic 
stakeholder roles.  Translating these generic roles into specific roles possessed by an organization is 
crucial for operational efficiency. Generic roles, while useful for defining broad responsibilities, may not 
align perfectly with the unique structure, capabilities, and expertise within an organization. By mapping 
these roles to specific positions, it is ensured that tasks are assigned to the most suitable individuals. 
This specificity enhances accountability, as it is clear who is responsible for what, and improves 
communication by aligning expectations with actual job functions within the organization. Moreover, it 
allows for more accurate resource planning and utilization, reduces redundancy, and helps in identifying 
any gaps in coverage.  
As a result, RoviSys should discuss with the customer project manager and relevant project team 
members to ensure that the generic roles for which communication is requested is translated to the 
specific roles and responsibilities within the customer's organization while working to identify the key 
individuals for which involvement is requested, rather than simply pass the generic templates to the 
customer and ask for these to be filled in.

Infrastructure Evaluation
The degree of infrastructure evaluation will depend based upon the ultimate goal of the organization.  
An MES/MOM -centric effort requires a high -level review of the underlying shop floor infrastructure, 
considering factors of importance when selecting and deploying such an application.  Factors to consider 
during such an evaluation include the following:
General network architecture, including shop floor and enterprise network delineation -
Network coverage on the shop floor, including support for wired and wireless devices-
Ability to send/receive data from the shop floor, including existing OPC or MQTT pipelines-
Existence of a historian layer-
Ability to integrate the shop floor and enterprise network layers to cloud -hosted applications -
Existence of terminals / clients on the shop floor that may be reused-
An infrastructure -specific discovery effort that would be commonly completed by the RoviSys BIIT team 
will require a deeper, more methodological analysis.  (Published) MES RIS 101.3 -Infrastructure Evaluation

aid in an understanding of current plant processes, constraints, and opportunities for replacement or 
augmentation.  Legacy system replacement is often a key aspect of the business case / ROI for a 
digitalization initiative, so it is important to perform a thorough review to be in a position to make 
recommendations concerning the path forward.  
Prior to any workshop or sessions, an inventory of legacy applications should be created by working with 
key customer IT / OT subject matter experts.  The following is a listing of general information to be 
captured as part of this inventory:
Application Name-
Site-
Plant Area-
Age-
Vendor (or home -grown) -
General Function-
Criticality (mission critical to production, helpful to production, unnecessary to production, etc.)-
Primary User Interface (web client, thick client, mobile, hosted within Office application such as 
Access or Excel, etc.)-
Primary SME (who can assist with demos and other questions)-
Support Status (actively supported by vendor/creator, vendor/creator support available, no 
support available)-
External interfaces / interactions with other applications-
External interfaces / interactions with underlying automation layer-
Master data management / configuration considerations (how is the application configured, who 
maintains it, what processes exist concerning master/configuration data management?)-
Any documentation available from existing applications should be obtained as part of legacy 
documentation review (MES RIS 101.7).  This may include user manuals, design documentation, 
troubleshooting guides, and other resources.  If possible, these documents should be qualified by the 
customer to confirm how up -to-date and accurate they are felt to be.  This documentation should be 
reviewed prior to any interactive demo.  
Any questions on unclear or poorly documented functionality can be captured from this documentation 
review and raised to the customer during the interactive demonstration.  
RoviSys can then arrange a demonstration of each application with the primary SME or delegate.  It will 
not be feasible during such a demonstration to document every single function, and this may not even 
be useful as the goal of a digitalization initiative is typically not to provide a one for one replacement of 
the legacy application stack.  Rather, general application functionality and usability should be captured, 
including the following key aspects:
How do users access and log into the application?-
Speed and responsiveness of the application, to baseline expectations of any new toolset-
Business logic / functions implemented within the application-
Data obtained from the application, including any reports, dashboards, and metrics-(Published) MES RIS 101.4 -Legacy System Review

Order of Review:
The condensed timeline of a DxDiscovery effort may not permit time for detailed review of everything 
provided.  Therefore, typically the most digestible documents should be reviewed first, and lengthy 
detailed documentation digested as time permits.  A general strategy is as follows:
Review process flows, layouts, and architectures to become acquainted with the plant layout, 
process flow, and infrastructure constraints-
Review production paperwork and schedule examples, as these will likely lead to questions and 
clarifications that will need to be discussed during the workshop sessions-
Review reporting examples, as these are also likely to lead to questions and clarifications that will 
need to be discussed during the workshop sessions-
User manuals and training documents will provide insight as to application functionality and user 
work processes-
Lastly, functional and design documents may be reviewed as time permits, but these documents 
are likely to take the most time to digest and are most likely to contain inaccuracies as they are 
often not updated as changes and enhancements are made.  -

Site Walk Evaluation
A plant tour / site walk is often conducted early during the assessment workshop.  The plant tour helps 
give the assessment team perspective concerning the actual constraints and processes conducted on 
the shop floor.  It is important to maximize the value of the site walk, as opportunities to spend time on 
the shop floor are typically few.
Safety Considerations:
First and foremost, it is important to conduct site walks in a safe manner.  There are inherent risks with 
being on the factory floor in an unfamiliar environment.  Some key considerations include the following:
Verify personal protective equipment (PPE) requirements prior to arriving onsite.  Safety shoes 
should be purchased prior and brought to site.  A hard hat, safety vest, safety glasses, and hearing 
protection are other typical requirements.  These can be brought to site but are usually made 
available by the customer.  Some sites may require long -sleeve shirts or may provide protective 
sleeves to wear.  Sites maintaining a certain sanitation level may require wearing gowns, hair nets, 
and beard nets.  -
It is likely that jewelry (watches, rings, earrings, etc.) will need to be removed prior to the site 
walk.  -
When walking the site, stay alert and close to the tour guide.  
Always yield to fork truck drivers and make eye contact / acknowledge the driver before 
crossing in the path of a fork truck○
Yield to automated guides vehicles○
Stay within designated pedestrian walkways○-
Watch for light curtains and physical e -stop gates.  Do not cross these, as it may put you at risk as 
well as shut down a line or piece of equipment.-
Avoid loose -fitting clothing and take care to ensure clothing or hair do not come in close contact 
with moving equipment.  -
Do not touch equipment or products unless explicitly given permission by your tour guide.  In -
process product can be hot, sharp, or caustic.  Touching may also contaminate the product.  -
Watch for trip hazards and take care on stairs and overhead walkways.-
Note taking can be difficult while moving through the facility.  If an important note needs to be 
taken, ask the tour guide to pause / stop while this is recorded.  -
Pre Site Walk:
It is useful to go over the process in -person or virtually prior to the site walk to better understand 
the process steps, production flow, line and equipment configuration, quality -centric activities, 
and other factors.  This information can be difficult to convey in full while on the tour and a review 
prior to the site walk can help give focus to specific activities of interest.  
Any process flow or plant layout documents that may be available can aid in this review.  
Ask if the plant has any such documents available.  ○-
Ask that the site walk / plant tour be done sequentially based on the order of production rather 
than based on the physical plant layout or convenience.  Conducting the site walk in a sequential 
manner will lessen confusion. -

During the Site Walk:
Be sure to ask or note questions.  It can be difficult to speak / discuss while on the plant floor due 
to noise.  Have a means of noting follow -up questions (such as a small notebook) and raise these

It is useful to talk to personnel on the floor, such as operators, quality technicians, maintenance

Tour guides and personnel will often focus the discussion on the manufacturing process itself,

important than this is a discussion of 'people processes' and 'system processes, including the

How do individuals know what to do next○
What electronic systems are leveraged on the line○
What common issues occur on the line and how are these issues resolved○-
Ensure explicit permission has been granted to take pictures or even have cell phones on the floor.  
Some sites prohibit the presence of electronic devices on the floor and picture taking due to 
intellectual property concerns.  In some cases, the tour guide or another member of the customer 
team may be able to take pictures on our behalf as instructed.  -
Do not take product from the shop floor unless explicit permission is given, including product 
perceived as scrap/waste.  -

Operations Management Capability Review
In many cases, a customer may be unfamiliar with the capabilities provided by an MES or MOM 
application, and there may be confusion as to the scope of the initiative as a result.  Even customers 
familiar with the digitalization of operations management functions may lack a deep understanding of 
capabilities provided by the different layers in the ISA -95 model, considering such systems as ERP, 
MES/MOM, SCADA, etc.  During this activity, RoviSys provides an overview of the capabilities provided 
as part of a digitalized ISA -95 compliant solution stack, focusing particularly on Level 3 capabilities most 
often provided by Layer 3 applications.  
To facilitate this exercise, a standard capabilities map has been defined, which can be found at the 
following link:
RoviSys S95 capability example.pptx
This can be reviewed with the customer to aid in understanding what capabilities are often found within 
the various levels.  The focus of a digitalization assessment is largely on Level 3, although other RoviSys 
services as a product (SaaP) offerings may also cover levels 1 & 2.  
Using the generic RoviSys capability map as a guideline, the following associated exercises can be 
conducted with the customer:  
The customer can be educated as to the core capabilities typically provided by a digitalization 
stack, specifically Level 3 operations management capabilities relevant to the assessment effort.  
Misconceptions as to what should be contained within the layers and associated systems such as 
SCADA, ERP, and MES can also be resolved during this review.  -
The capabilities can be reviewed with the customer to ensure alignment of naming.  The customer 
may require the capability in question, but refer to it by a different name.  Therefore, it is 
important to discuss each capability with the customer rather than simply present the various 
terms, to eliminate any misunderstandings.  -
Any legacy systems leveraged by the customer to provide each capability can be captured, 
allowing for the creation of a legacy application map that will help to guide the remainder of the 
assessment.  -
RoviSys can work with the customer to prioritize certain capabilities of focus based upon this high -
level information.  For example, struggles with a legacy system or lack of an automated system to 
provide a certain capability may cause a certain capability to be prioritized over others.  -
Based on this discussion, a revised capability map can be provided specific to the customer, ensuring 
that relevant capabilities are shown, capabilities are named according to customer vernacular, legacy 
systems providing the capabilities are overlaid, and specific prioritizations are highlighted.  
A customer unfamiliar with MES / MOM may benefit from viewing a demo of a typical MES / MOM 
solution.  There is some risk in providing a demo to the customer that the demo environment will not 
look and feel like the customer's operation, causing confusion or loss of interest.  As a result, RoviSys 
should strive to draw parallels to how the demonstrated functionality could be applied to the 
customer's enterprise, and should work with the demo presenter to make the demo as realistic and 
topical as possible.  (Published) MES RIS 101.8 -Operations Management

Current Process State Definition
This effort helps to baseline the current state of the facility or facilities under the scope of the 
assessment.  This exercise gives RoviSys background concerning current shop floor activities and system -
level processes that will help to frame the rest of the assessment effort, including specific topics to 
discuss and questions to ask during stakeholder interviews.  
The following are typical means by which RoviSys gathers current process state information:
Documentation Review:
The customer may possess legacy documentation that can be reviewed in an offline manner.  This 
includes user manuals, SOPs, piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs), swimlane diagrams, process 
flows, etc.  Early in the assessment initiative RoviSys should formulate an ask for such documentation.  
However, care must be taken not to spend too much time reviewing legacy documentation that may be 
incorrect or may be cumbersome / confusing when a more direct means of obtaining the same 
information (site tours, stakeholder reviews, etc.) may be more efficient.  
Conference Room Overview:
During this session, the customer walks RoviSys through the manufacturing process, including key user 
and/or system touchpoints.  It can be advantageous to discuss how the site / enterprise operates in a 
conference room setting prior to the site tour as it is easier to communicate and ask questions in a 
meeting setting than on the floor with noise and other distractions.  This discussion provides a baseline 
for the site tour that allows more useful details to be gathered during the tour.  
Site Tour:
The primary goal of a site tour is not to understand the customer's manufacturing and supporting 
business processes, as this information can be more easily obtained offline.  Rather, the site tour helps 
to establish perspective that may weigh into the subsequent business intentions and business process 
scenarios.  Some examples include the following:
The speed at which production moves on the shop floor-
Locations at which manual operations occur or areas where key data may be captured in an 
automated manner-
The size and scale of the facility, which may necessitate or eliminate certain solution options (such 
as mobile devices, vision systems, etc.)-
The scope of an operator's tasks-
Opportunities for overhead visualizations, stack lights, paging, and other notification conduits-
Locations where whiteboards or bulletin boards may exist to capture or convey information that 
could be replaced with a digital system-
Usage of paper work instructions-
Methods of identifying raw materials, WIP product, and finished goods (labels, barcodes, etc.)-
The site tour can also help to highlight concerns that can be discussed during the stakeholder interview 
process, including the following examples:(Published) MES RIS 101.9 -Current Process State Definition

Large buildups of staged WIP product between stations-
Lines / machines not running-

Paper -based operations (tickets, travelers, labels, etc.) -
Inefficient work processes (Operator has to walk large distances to complete tasks, perform

Lastly, the site tour can permit access to speak to operators, supervisors, quality techs, etc. first hand to 
gain insights concerning how these individuals perform their daily work, concerns, or ideas they may 
have for improvement.  The tour will not allow every scenario to be captured but allows us to hear what 
top of mind for these individuals.  Additionally, it helps to build early relationships and impressions that 
we are at the site to help, not hurt operations.  
If possible ask the customer to execute the site tour based upon the product flow sequence, rather than 
convenience of other factors.  This reduces confusion and helps us relate the tour to the process 
overview previously discussed.  
Legacy System Review:
Often, legacy systems can be shown in a conference room or web conference setting.  The customer can 
provide a high -level overview of the various functions supported by the legacy systems, information 
provided, and can highlight specific  challenges, bugs, or gaps.  The time taken to load or save data can 
be captured as a rough baseline.  Note that the goal of a digitalization initiative is rarely to duplicate a 
legacy system function -for-function, but a legacy system review can help highlight what works well and 
what does not.  
Current Process State Documentation:
Conference room and web -based reviews should be recorded and transcribed if at all possible.  Seek the 
customer's permission prior to recording, and provide any recordings captured to the customer after the 
sessions.
Taking pictures of the shop floor may be permitted, but always seek the customer's permission before 
taking photos.  In some cases cameras and other recording devices are not permitted on the shop floor 
or explicit authorization must be secured prior.  In other cases, the customer may be able to take photos 
and provide them.  
If permitted by the customer, bring a lightweight notebook and writing utensil on the plant tour to jot 
down key notes or ideas.  
A designated notetaker is useful during conference room walkthroughs and legacy application reviews 
to ensure that key facts are not missed as the leader of the meeting is focused on driving the 
conversation and asking questions.  Notes should be cleaned up and provided to the customer after the 
sessions.  
Executing legacy application reviews over web conference allow screen captures or videos of legacy 
applications to be taken.  
It can be useful in the assessment to provide a concise summarization of learnings, including a process 
overview, the role of legacy applications, and major concerns / pain points captured during 
observations.  The customer knows their process, so this is not the primary benefit/focus of the 
assessment.  Rather, this documentation shows the customer that RoviSys understands their process,

Stakeholder Group Interview Process
Purpose:
The stakeholder interview process is important to gain insights facilitating formulation of the 'to -be' 
business process scenarios.  The goal of this exercise is to better understand the role of each 
stakeholder in the manufacturing process, then apply our knowledge of digitalization / MES to 
recommend altered work processes that are likely to provide tangible benefits.  The goal of the exercise 
is NOT for the stakeholder to tell us what those future processes should be.  Stakeholders may have 
opinions concerning various aspects of their daily work, data they wish was more accessible, systems 
that they wish had better user interfaces, etc., and it is important to capture that feedback.  However,  
stakeholders often will not realize that there is a better way to do what they are doing, and the 
customer is paying RoviSys to help identify those insights as part of the assessment.  
The stakeholder group interviews should minimize the time required of both the stakeholders and 
ourselves.  Therefore, these interviews must be properly planned, efficiently executed, and effectively 
documented.  
Current Process State Background:
Ideally, preliminary conversations with the customer project team concerning the goals of the initiative, 
the workflows within the organization, and various plant personnel should provide sufficient 
background to give us an understanding of who we want to talk to and what we want to find out more 
about.  Use this exercise to formulate the scope of the stakeholder interviews.  The size and scope of the 
assessment effort will also come into play.  For example, if we are focusing on a maintenance initiative 
in a certain area it may not be as worthwhile to talk to quality personnel in an unrelated area.  
Stakeholder Group Identification:    
The various groups we desire to interview must first be identified.  Customers often have different 
names for different groups and roles within the organization, so we must coordinate with our project 
contacts to understand these groups / roles.  The following is a generic list of the various groups we 
generally desire to interview:
Plant Manager-
Production Managers-
Controls Engineers-
IT / Manufacturing IT-
Finance / Business Analysts-
Schedulers-
Receiving-
Area Managers / Leads-
Warehouse Managers-
Quality Managers-
Process Engineers-
Maintenance Managers-

Stakeholder Identification:
Depending on the role, it may be impractical to talk to all individuals in the organization.  Therefore, we 
must collaborate with our project contacts who must in turn collaborate with others in the organization 
to identify the key individuals to be interviewed, based upon factors such as seniority, knowledge, and 
communication skills.  Identifying a stakeholder that can speak to multiple areas can lead to time 
efficiencies.  
It is often beneficial to interview several individuals in small groups to avoid redundancy and save time 
during the process.  We should typically avoid interview meetings with large groups of unrelated 
individuals though.  The larger the group setting, the less likely some individuals will be to provide 
insights, while others may be more likely to posture or overstate certain aspects.  
Additional Site Inclusion:
Even if the scope of the project is limited to one site in a multi -site corporation, consideration should be 
given to visiting / interviewing other sites to ensure that a global solution is defined, rather than one 
that only meets the needs of the site in question.  
Agenda Formulation:
We want to be as minimally disruptive as possible to the day -to-day jobs of the individuals we identify to 
interview.  Therefore, sessions should be scheduled based on availability and kept as short as possible.  
Typically 1 -2 hours is the maximum amount of time that can be expected for a specific stakeholder / 
stakeholder group interview session.  
A typical DxDiscovery stakeholder interview agenda for a specific manufacturing site is around 2 -3 days 
in duration.  The following document reference contains a sample agenda:
Sample DxDiscovery Agenda_Questions.xlsx
Our customer project contact should be able to look at calendars and help find specific times during 
which specific stakeholder groups are available.  
The above document reference also contains sample interview questions for each stakeholder group 
that can be tailored based on the customer, industry, and other factors, and included in the meeting 
invites.  
Meeting Invites:
We do not want customer stakeholders to feel like they need to perform a large degree of preparation 
prior to the interview sessions.  However, it is useful to include sample interview questions in the 
invites, along with any other specific requests.  For example, we may want a participant to demonstrate 
a legacy system, bring log sheets or work instruction samples, or perform other prework.  This prework 
should be clearly stated in the invites so time is not wasted obtaining this information during the session 
or waiting for follow -ups to be performed.
Interview Execution:
It is okay for the conversation to drift off script in certain cases, and this can be useful to gain insights 
concerning associated processes and systems that may not be under the scope of the initiative if

Workshop Wrap -Up:
At the end of each workshop day, the next day's agenda should be reviewed with the customer team, 
including any session or time changes due to either customer resource availability or prior sessions that 
ran long / short, and the expected attendees to confirm their availability.  Open actions / parking lot 
items should also be reviewed, including prioritization, follow -up date, and assigned responsible party.  
A responsible party should be assigned if an action requires follow -up and one was not assigned during 
the capture of the item.  This may require customer project team input or follow -up.   
At the end of the workshop, next steps should be reviewed, including the need to schedule follow -ups, 
notes / documentation to be provided, and RoviSys deliverables to be provided based upon the 
workshop findings.    
Interview Documentation:
At a minimum, the RoviSys team should consist of the interviewer, who is focused on asking prompting 
questions and driving forward the session, and a note taker, who is focused on the capture of 
information.  Additionally, it is recommended that sessions be recorded so that unclear discussions can 
be replayed during our subsequent review.  In an in -person setting, an omnidirectional microphone can 
facilitate recording in an inobtrusive manner.    
Post interview, the notes from the sessions should be read through to ensure understanding and 
sanitized.  Some customers will explicitly ask for the notes from the sessions but it is good practice to 
send them to the customer, even if not explicitly requested.  Additionally, customers should be provided 
with any recordings that were taken.

Perceived Benefit
The goal of the DxDiscovery effort is to gather sufficient information to aid the customer in making a 
high -level recommendation as to the best path forward to facilitate improvement.  Several typical 
options are as follows:
Execution of a DxArchitecture effort to better define the manner in which digitalization can be 
applied to improve plant processes, efficiency, quality-
Execution of a DxArchitecture effort to better define the manner in which digitalization can be 
applied to replace obsolete or disconnected systems-
Execution of a DxLean effort to identify plant process improvements that can increase efficiency 
and reduce waste, independent of a digitalization effort-
Problems and potential outcomes may possess sufficient clarify that a pilot implementation 
initiative can be proposed-
Proposal of a full digitalization initiative, including architecture, implementation, and deployment-
Execution of a deeper controls / automation front -end engineering design (FEED) effort to define

showing the system responsible for each activity, as well as system -to-system interactions or user -to-
system interactions.  This activity is especially useful to facilitate a technical team's understanding of the 
role of various systems and how they fit together.  The process activity diagram highlights areas where 
detailed system interface design will be required, as well as cases where user interfaces will need to be 
made available.  These diagrams can be particularly useful when a customer possesses existing legacy 
systems and is struggling to picture how the MES / MOM initiative will fit into the overall systems

The first step in creation of a process activity diagram is identification of the distinct systems and roles

Usually the diagram does not need to go to the level of showing specific modules within systems.  This

process control systems coming first, then historian, MES, and lastly enterprise systems.

Business Process Scenario Definition (SIPOC)
Purpose:
Business process scenarios capture high level details concerning the various activities (processes) 
envisioned to be executed within the manufacturing enterprise, once digitalization is applied. 
The goals of the defined business process scenarios include the following:
Be easily understood by non -technical stakeholders -
Be documented in an efficient, repeatable manner as part of the assessment process-
Be technology agnostic.  The business process scenario should refer to various business systems at 
a high level (MES, ERP, LIMS, control system, etc.), but not delve into the nuances of applying a 
specific platform or technical solution-
Establish 'guardrails' concerning the solution to be provided, so that the intended processes to be 
facilitated by the solution are clear, reducing the possibility of future scope creep
Both typical (sunny day) and exception (rainy day) scenarios should be captured○-
Provide a basis upon which more detailed user stories can be built.  User stories should be 
matrixed to business process scenarios so that the goal and reasoning for each user story is clear-
Highlight required user -to-system and system -to-system interactions, which can be leveraged 
when building more detailed technical documentation (architecture diagrams, value stream maps, 
etc.)-
The functionality basis established by the business process scenarios assists not only with up -front 
understanding of the scope of the solution and value to be provided, but also serves as a basis for future 
implementation and deployment activities.  For example, properly -defined business process scenarios 
can serve as a foundation for testing plans (integration testing, FAT, UAT, etc.) and creation of role -
specific training materials such as SOPs.  Therefore, it is important to keep defined business process 
scenarios up -to-date throughout the initiative so that they can be utilized later in the project lifecycle, 
further enhancing their value.  
Methodology:
The MES division has adopted the 'SIPOC' methodology for the definition of business process scenarios.  
This is an industry standard methodology that has been adapted to better serve the needs of our MES 
project initiatives.  
S = Process suppliers

P = Process
O = Process outputs
C = Process consumers

Usage of SIPOC to Capture Decision Points
Background:
A key consideration when documenting business process scenarios is to properly distill decision points 
throughout the process leveraging the SIPOC format, including all inputs needed to support the decision, 
the process entailed in making the decision, and resulting decision output.  
This is particularly applicable to life sciences digitalization deployments, as the primary driver for the 
initiative is ultimately to support product release by exception.  This necessitates exception scenarios / 
anomalies to be identified and resolved throughout the process, then reviewed subsequent to making a 
final decision concerning the ability of the product to be released to the consumer.  However, a goal of 
digitalization in general is to enable decision makers, and thus it is important for these decision points to 
be properly distilled and agreed upon as part of business process scenario definition.  
Longer -term, if these decision points are properly captured and clearly defined, agentic systems may be 
applied to support decision making, reducing human intervention.  These systems can determine 
specifically when human feedback is required, present targeted information supporting the decision 
making process so that the human need not spend time mining data from disparate data sources, and 
may ultimately be able to make certain decisions autonomously.  Therefore, proper documentation of 
all decision points is essential to future support for such agentic systems.  
SIPOC Hierarchy:
Decision points may warrant creation of dedicated child SIPOC diagrams that are related to higher -
level parents.  For example, there may be an overall SIPOC driving product release upon 
production completion.  This SIPOC may be fed by the output of numerous child SIPOCs, 
representing smaller decision points that feed into the overall product release decision.  For 
example, exception scenarios may arise throughout production warranting scrapping a batch, 
reworking an assembly, or moving forward due to the high likelihood that the product will still be 
compliant.  These decisions must be reviewed and determined to be of no risk to product safety 
prior to the distribution of the product to the consumer.  -
Input and Decision Considerations:
The SIPOC author must ensure that all inputs needed to support the decision in question are 
captured.  This may include both immediate data points created in the context of the batch / 
assembly in question, as well as contextual and historical data from other products / batches / 
production runs that may be needed by a person or agent to properly make a decision.  Some 
examples include the following:-
If a dimensional check fails, measuring equipment calibration records may need to be 
consulted to confirm that the measuring device was properly calibrated within the proper 
time thresholds.  The act of reviewing these records and making a decision should be 
captured as part of the SIPOC documentation process, and the decision made (recalibrate 
and retest the part, fail the part, pass the part, etc.) captured as an output.  ○(Published) MES RIS 102.4.1 -Usage of SIPOC to Capture 
Decision Points
Tuesday, January 28, 2025 8:10 AM
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 49    
and retest the part, fail the part, pass the part, etc.) captured as an output.  
If a part or material is leveraged that was not indicated on the BOM, supplier records, 
including the CoA, may need to be consulted.  Perhaps a substitute part was sent by the 
supplier that possesses the same quality criteria and is an acceptable substitute?  Or, an 
inferior part may have been provided that will require the assembly to be rejected?○
A part may be sourced from multiple different suppliers, but historical data indicates that 
parts from a certain provider often lead to downstream quality issues.  Usage of the part 
from the suspect supplier may warrant additional quality verifications (additional 
dimensional checks, electrical checks, visual inspections, etc.) before release of the 
assembly.  ○
In the event that a batch exceeds some CTQ (critical to quality) parameter, such as a pH, 
temperature, etc., historical trend data may need to be consulted to look at the value over 
time.  Was the exceeded value an anomaly that was quickly brought back into conformance, 
or has the historical data point been trending in the wrong direction for some time?  The 
latter is indicative of a larger issue that should be resolved and may necessitate scrapping 
the batch, while the former may be acceptable should subsequent testing prove that the 
batch ultimately meets all established quality criteria.  ○
An improper amount of a certain raw material may have been added, which requires 
consultation with a staff chemist to determine if the raw material addition error will lead to 
a potency issue or presents a risk to patient safety.  The chemist may be required to perform 
additional lab tests or consult historical data from patient trials to make such determination.  ○
Denotation:
Consideration should be given to breaking out decision making processes, particularly those 
requiring multiple inputs and/or sequential decision making steps, into their own SIPOC diagrams 
for ease of review and understanding.  -
All inputs (direct or indirect) required to support the decision should be captured, including the 
source / supplier of the input.  Consideration must be given not only to input values that are 
immediately accessible as part of the specific product's production, but also indirect or historical 
inputs that may need to be obtained by the decision maker to utilize in making a judgement call 
concerning product quality.    -
An output that is either a supporting decision point that feeds a higher -level SIPOC or ultimately a 
decision point concerning the quality of a finished product should be clearly denoted as such.  -

Generic Architecture
The generic architecture shows the various interactions envisioned between systems as well as 
touchpoints between people and systems (clients, scanners, instruments, etc.), agnostic of a specific 
digitalization platform.  This documentation aids in understanding how the MES/MOM platform stack 
will fit into the overall enterprise systems landscape, and can help better visualize architectural 
constraints that may need to be considered when performing technology selection activities.  
There are two common processes leveraged to document a generic architecture.  One or both of these 
may be of use to generate and provide to the customer during the assessment phase.  
Block Diagram:
A block diagram shows specific systems or system placeholders and associated interconnections 
between them.  The block diagram is often organized according to the ISA -95 hierarchy:
ERP-
MES / MOM-
SCADA / HMI-
Controls-
Legacy systems and applications expected to remain within the solution stack can be explicitly called 
out, while placeholders for new applications can be referenced generically.  Additionally, it can be useful 
to document 'before and after' block diagrams, showing the existing systems landscape and to -be 
systems landscape after legacy applications are decommissioned and/or new functionality is 
incorporated.   
The block diagram may also convey boundaries between on -premises, cloud, and corporate 
applications, network delineations (controls network, site business network, corporate network), and 
other aspects related to infrastructure (like user interface types and locations).  
A complex architecture and associated block diagram is not always better.  Rather, steps should be 
taken to simplify the architecture wherever possible, and the generic architecture exercise can help to 
highlight cases where the architecture envisioned is overly complex.  For example, a large number of 
crisscrossed point -to-point interfaces could be replaced by a centralized data pipeline / universal 
namespace (UNS) that follows more of a hub and spoke architecture.

Technology Selection Process
The result of the technology selection activity is clarity concerning the solution stack that will be 
leveraged to deliver on the envisioned process scenarios and corresponding ROI.  A variety of 
measurable criteria are evaluated to ensure that there is a solid justification for the technology 
selection(s) made.  
Technology Platform Shortlist:
The first step in executing the technology assessment is shortlisting the platforms to be evaluated.  If 
RoviSys was contracted directly by the customer to perform an independent analysis, we have the 
opportunity to select and rate various competing platform solutions.  However, if RoviSys was brought 
into the opportunity by a vendor, we may not be afforded this opportunity.  In this case, the technology 
assessment should focus on how to best utilize the vendor platform and where weaknesses in the 
vendor platform may require supplemental components that RoviSys can recommend due to our 
independence.  
Given the hundreds of platforms and niche solutions on the market, it is impractical to evaluate every 
option.  Rather, our experience is applied to first recommend a set of short -listed candidates.  Typically, 
the shortlist is comprised of the following:
MES priority platforms that we feel may have merit as the basis for the solution.  This is based 
upon industry, functional requirements,  manufacturing type (batch, continuous, discrete), and 
required interfaces to external systems.  The MES Platform Highlights register is a valuable 
resource when determining applicable shortlisted platforms:

A custom development alternative may also warrant inclusion in some cases.  Particularly, the 
customer may desire a custom -developed solution to be considered, or the scope of the 
deployment may yield benefits that outweigh the higher development and maintenance costs of a 
custom option.  For example, a customer possessing 100 sites may see a custom option with no

with a handful of sites.    -
Some solutions may inherently be non -starters due to certain aspects.  For example, a cloud or SaaS

Criteria Definition:
The criteria to be utilized include a mix of general solution capabilities, vendor stability and reliability, 
and aspects specific to the functionality required to fulfill the various business process scenarios.  
Criteria should be grouped into overall categories.  
Generic categories to be considered include the following:
Business Fit: 
These criteria rank the selected options based upon their applicability to the customer's 
manufacturing type, vendor and integrator presence in regions / continents aligning to the 
customer manufacturing plant footprint, evidence that the vendor solution has been applied in 
situations of similar scale / complexity, and vendor stability (ongoing investment in solution, 
financial stability, etc.)-
User Experience Fit:
These criteria rank the user experiences provided by the selected options, including required form 
factors (web, mobile, etc.), robustness of the out -of-the-box user experiences provided by the 
platform, and ability to extend the user interfaces to provide visualizations unique to the 
customer.  -
Functional Capability Fit:
These criteria rank each solution according to its ability to deliver needed functionality based upon 
the defined business process scenarios.  A platform may possess screens, workflows, and event 
models that correlate well to the needed functionality, or provide a solid foundation upon which 
the functionality can be built.  It is important to think about how the platform can be leveraged 
specific to the business process scenario.  For example, many platforms generically support 
schedule execution, but a certain specific platform may be well suited to a scenario in which 
multiple orders possessing the same container type can be consolidated and treated as one larger 
order at a filler.  The advice of RoviSys solution SMEs or solution architects may be warranted to 
assist with this ranking exercise.  -
External Systems Integration Fit:
These criteria rank each solution according to its ability to integrate to external systems according 
to the envisioned generic architecture.  A certain solution may provide a specific interface as -is, or 
provide a solid framework for the creation of the interface.  -
Technical Implementation Fit:
These criteria rank each solution in terms of the ease of maintenance and deployment.  
Availability of vendor technical support conduits, product documentation, an established technical 
support community, as well as support for modern development, troubleshooting, and testing 
methodologies are all considerations in this section. -
Solution Deployment Flexibility Fit: 
These criteria rank ease of deployment for each shortlisted option.  This includes solution 
alignment to the customer's preferred hosting model (on -premises, cloud, SaaS, etc.) the -

alignment to the customer's preferred hosting model (on -premises, cloud, SaaS, etc.) the 
magnitude of infrastructure required and associated cost, and other factors such as the ability of 
the solution to host multiple site implementations within a single instance.  Other deployment 
considerations include ease of solution installation and patching, disaster recovery and 
redundancy functionality, as well as support for complementary data warehousing or data lake 
solutions.  
Solution Cost:
These criteria rank ease solution in terms of cost.  This includes simplicity of the vendor costing 
model, scalability of the cost model, anticipated licensing cost relative to its peers, anticipated 
maintenance cost relative to its peers, and anticipated services cost relative to its peers.  For 
example, a low -cost solution with limited out -of-the-box capabilities may prove to possess a 
higher cost in the long run than a high -cost solution with rich out -of-the-box capabilities.  Solution 
cost is one area where a scaling factor larger than 0 -5 may be justified.  For example, a solution in 
a different order of magnitude ballpark may warrant scaling at the high end of a 0 -10 spectrum to 
better highlight the pricing differential. -
Scaling Factor Definition:
A scaling factor is then established against which each technology option is ranked.  For example, a 
rating of 5 may indicate an option is an excellent fit, while 0 indicates no fit (function not achievable 
within the platform, even with customization).  A scale of 1 -5 is generally appropriate for the purposes 
of the ranking.  A larger scale such as 1 -10 can be unwieldy, as it can be difficult to quantify subtle 
differences (such as between a 6 and a 7).   
Weighting Factor Definition:
Each category is assigned a weighting factor based upon the importance of a given area from both 
RoviSys' and the customer's perspectives.  Functional fit is typically assigned the highest weighting, as 
the most important aspect of the solution is its ability to fulfill the envisioned business process 
scenarios.  However, an extremely cost -conscious customer may weight cost more heavily than user 
experience fit.  External system integration may not be as important to a customer with a limited 
external solution stack.  
Criteria within a category may also be weighted and a weighted average calculated to arrive at an 
overall average score for the category.  Otherwise, a straight average of the scores within the category is 
taken to arrive at an overall score for the category.  
A weighted average of all category scores can then be taken to arrive at an overall score for each option.  
Freeform Comments:
It is useful to provide comments and explanations describing why certain criteria were ranked in a given 
manner.  This can be useful for reference or when reviewing the scorecard with the customer.

ROI Guidance Formulation
It is important to provide our customers guidance concerning how the solutions we propose will provide 
a return on investment (ROI).  It is generally beyond our capabilities to calculate the ROI for our 
customers in a vacuum, as we lack specific knowledge on various costs including raw materials, finished 
goods, labor, etc.  However, we can provide guidelines and examples that our customers can leverage, 
allowing them to plug in financial numbers to determine expected ROI. 
Note that ROI calculations are approximations.  We should err on being conservative with our 
estimations so that customer expectations are managed throughout the initiative.    
There are three primary types of ROI that should be considered:
Legacy system infrastructure and maintenance cost reduction-
Tangible ROI-
Calamity avoidance ROI-
These three considerations are broken down in the following sections.
Legacy System Infrastructure and Maintenance:
Often, MES initiatives are justified due to infrastructure and IT support savings.  Some potential 
considerations include the following:
Reduction in licensing and recurring vendor support costs due to legacy application elimination or 
consolidation-
Reduction in physical infrastructure cost due to consolidation of legacy servers, migration to the 
cloud, removal of costly mainframe systems, or transition from thick clients (physical PCs) to web 
or thin clients-
Reduction in IT / OT support staff due to reduction in the application portfolio requiring upkeep 
and troubleshooting-
Removal of unstable systems requiring frequent intervention to keep running-
Elimination of physical interfaces requiring specialized network hardware, wiring, etc. -
Tangible ROI:
Tangible ROI is based upon direct cost savings due to implementation of new processes enabled by the 
MES platform.  Note that installing the MES platform itself does not provide a tangible ROI.  Rather, the 
efficiencies gained by the new work processes facilitated by the MES are what provide the benefit.  
Therefore, it is important to properly define and manage these work process changes alongside the 
deployment of the MES itself.  
Some examples of tangible ROI include the following:
Reduction in time spent inputting data into the system or running reports to find insights.-
Direct interfaces to external systems such as ERP allowing data to be transferred in real -time 
rather than relying upon manual data transposition-
Direct interfaces to shop floor devices, ensuring that product and recipe information is conveyed -(Published) MES RIS 102.8 -ROI Guidance Formulation

Direct interfaces to shop floor devices, ensuring that product and recipe information is conveyed 
in real -time with less potential for data entry error-
Access to work instructions, changeover procedures, or other information allowing manual tasks 
to be completed more efficiently or accurately, leading to greater production uptime or increased 
first-pass yield-
Optimization algorithms allowing greater throughput due to shop floor schedule optimization and 
resulting increased capacity-
Greater insight into poorly performing lines or work cells, allowing work processes to be enacted 
to more quickly achieve an ideal production state, increasing the overall equipment effectiveness 
(OEE) of the facility-
Reduction in safety stock, in -flight WIP, or raw material inventory, in turn increasing working 
capital-
Standardization of processes, reducing site -or area -specific training demands and ensuring all 
personnel complete a task in the same manner-
Some aspects of tangible ROI may have a greater impact than others, depending on the customer, 
industry, and even region where the plant is located.  Reduction of manual processes may have a 
dramatic impact in a region where labor is expensive or difficult to secure, or the task is highly complex 
in nature, but may be negligible in an area where manpower is cheap and plentiful.  Raw material 
inventory reductions may lead to substantial savings if the cost of such raw materials is high, but if raw 
materials are cheap and easily obtained this may not be a factor.  
Engagement of the plant financial team is crucial during the ROI formulation exercise to ensure factors 
are taken into account that may not be known to the project team.  The finance team will have insights 
into labor, capital, and material costs that will allow for more accurate ROI formulation.  
Again, it is important to think of tangible costs savings from a work process perspective.  For example, 
deployment of an OEE dashboard to the facility will not lead to an automatic increase in OEE.  Rather, 
the enhanced visibility provided by the dashboards should trigger the execution of work processes that 
more quickly return the facility to producing good quality product at the target ideal rate.  
Manual OEE calculations or time studies may be required to be performed over a time period to 
determine where the plant currently operates and then cost savings projected based on this data.  For 
example, if the equipment is down two hours a day and it is felt that with proper visibility and triggering 
of associated downtime resolution work processes this downtime can be decreased to 1 hour a day, the 
additional output able to be realized in the extra hour of uptime is the tangible ROI.  
Calamity Avoidance ROI:
Calamity avoidance ROI is the most difficult to calculate because the impact is vague in nature, but often 
provides the greatest justification for the initiative.  This type of ROI is realized via avoidance of an 
incident that could severely impact the company, requiring money to be spent to resolve and/or 
reducing the company's sales.  There is a chance the incident may or may not occur even if the MES is 
put in place, but the goal of the MES platform is to act as an insurance policy of sorts, making the 
likelihood of occurrence far less than it otherwise would be.  
Some examples of calamity avoidance ROI include the following:
Prevention of an equipment failure that leads to a facility shutdown and substantial lost 
production-
Reduction in the likelihood of a recall scenario due to enactment of consistent quality procedures, 
such as periodic sample and test operations.  A recall scenario not only impacts cost of scrapped 
product that must be removed from the value stream and destroyed, but also impacts the 
company's reputation and could lead to consumer avoidance of the company's products -
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 59    
company's reputation and could lead to consumer avoidance of the company's products 
depending upon the severity.  
Containment of a quality issue or recall scenario due to availability of material genealogy data.  
For example, perhaps a specific raw material lot was the source of a quality issue.  The MES allows 
data to be quickly obtained concerning all finished goods leveraging that raw material lot.  -
Enforcement of operations that promote safety, such as preventing operators from performing 
tasks for which they lack qualifications or training.  Avoidance of operator injury or death prevents 
lawsuits as well as subsequent loss of reputation.-
Reduction in the likelihood of a cybersecurity issue, infrastructure obsolescence, or a support 
issue that could make legacy systems inoperable and halt operations for an indeterminate time 
period.  -
Calamity avoidance ROI is especially critical when dealing with life sciences MES initiatives.  These 
regulated industries require a full audit trail of both system and operator actions, an electronic record of 
batch production, and other aspects promoting traceability.  Lack of this information may make the 
enterprise more susceptible to FDA audit, potentially requiring costly remediations to be enacted in a 
quick manner, and forcing the company to halt production until such actions are taken.  
The customer may be able to cite previous incidents and the associated impact when assigning tangible 
dollars to calamity avoidance ROI.  Or, the customer may have already performed simulated studies 
concerning the impact of various recall or safety scenarios.  The customer may also need to use statistics 
and historical data to predict the likelihood of an incident over any given period.  For example, the 
customer may predict that a major recall is likely to occur every 10 years, with a 10 percent chance of a 
recall in any given year.  
Note that even a conservatively low estimate of the potential cost savings by incident avoidance is often 
enough to justify the money spent on the MES initiative.  
ROI Documentation Practices:
ROI should be tied back to specific business process scenarios and business intentions.  If a group of 
business process scenarios must be implemented in parallel to lead to the ROI, this should be 
documented so that the customer understands that they must implement all of the related business 
process scenarios before the ROI will be obtained.  A description of the recommended calculation 
should be provided, allowing the customer to define specific numbers based upon their business.  In 
some cases the customer may not want to disclose the specific numbers to RoviSys, which is okay.  What 
is of utmost importance is that the customer feels confident that the solution proposed will positively 
impact their bottom line to the extent that proceeding with the MES initiative is justified.  
ROI Payback Period:
The payback period is the duration in which the MES installation and associated services will be paid for, 
and after which all cost savings result in profit increase.  When prioritizing business process scenarios to 
be implemented, the ROI payback period should be considered to identify functionality that provides 
the greatest benefit in the shortest timeframe.  Finance should again be consulted to determine the 
company's priorities.  For example, it may be more desirable to implement functionality that yields an 
immediate $500K savings than one that will save the company $1MM after three years of runtime.
The MES software licensing model must also be considered when determining ROI.  A perpetual 
licensing model will require a greater up -front expenditure, but once 'paid off' by the ROI over some 
timespan, all additional savings are pure profit.  A subscription -based system must provide cost savings 
greater than the subscription cost over the subscription period in question to be financially viable, and 
uphold this savings over the lifespan of the MES.

Resource -Based Quotation Methodology
In some cases, a rough schedule and a listing of desired scope items may exist, but there is not enough 
task granularity to formulate a task -based quotation.  It may not be feasible to generate all the various 
tasks due to lack of clarity and/or lack of time.  In these cases, a strategy to give the customer an 
approximate budgetary estimate is to formulate a quotation based upon resource loading. 
Even if a task -based estimate is being created, formulation of a resource -based model can be a useful 
'cross -check' to ensure that the task estimates are realistic.  Task -based estimates tend to be light when 
one considers the full team that will be required to support the project over the course of the project's 
lifecycle.  A resource -based model may highlight areas that need to be bolstered.  
To formulate this style of quotation, first the calendar schedule is laid out (often within an Excel sheet).  
Calendar time may be represented generically (month one, month two, etc.) if the start date is unclear, 
or a starting date established and the calendar built upon this.  
Next, the calendar time within the schedule is split up according to envisioned project phases.  Key 
phases that may be represented include the following examples:
Assessment•
Project planning•
User story definition•
Sprint execution (x number of sprints envisioned)•
Sprint testing (x number of sprints envisioned)•
Sprint deployment•
Hypercare support•
The duration of a specific phase is approximated based upon the customer's schedule constraints and 
our experience in the time required to complete given tasks.  The customer may have a target go -live 
date aligned to a site startup, supporting system (such as ERP) cutover, or other factors.  In these cases, 
one can work backward from the go -live date to slot in the various activities above.  
Some timeline approximations are as follows:
A full assessment effort, including site visit, business process scenario definition, technology 
comparison, architecture formulation, roadmap formulation, and executive summary, typically  
requires between 6 and 8 weeks, although this time period can be compressed.  •
Detailed project planning is often a 2 -week effort •
User story definition may typically take between 1 and 2 weeks prior to the kickoff of each sprints
Definition of initial user stories must be done before the commencement of the first sprint.  
Thereafter, user story definition for the next sprint can overlap with execution and testing of 
the current sprint.  However, in the event of this overlap, sufficient architect and lead -level 
resources must be available to drive both the current and next sprint.  ○
There may be a desire to sequence user story development and sprint build/test in a 
sequential manner with no overlap.  However, consideration must be given in this scenario 
to ensure that the project developers have value -add tasks during user story development.  
Otherwise, it is impractical to ramp the development team on and off the project to keep 
them busy during user story definition.  ○•
Sprint execution is often 4 -6 weeks in duration, although this is dependent upon the complexity of 
the sprint.  It is at the estimator's discretion based on project scope and experience whether a 
larger number of shorter sprints (2 weeks for example) or a smaller number of longer sprints are 
better.  •
Sprint testing is often 2 weeks in duration.•
A tight schedule may require sprints to overlap with multiple workstreams involved.  This will in 
turn require additional resources to be allocated to support the overlapping sprints.  •
For a large -scale MES rollout, execution of the FAT and UAT activities for a full MES deployment, 
including remediation, may last between four and six weeks.  For example, one week for FAT, one 
week to resolve issues from FAT, one week for UAT, and one week to resolve issues from UAT.  •
Other testing periods may also be required, including regression testing, integration testing, 
performance testing, simulation testing, and other aspects.  •
Ample time should be allocated for deployment preparation and deployment activities•
Go-live and post deployment hypercare support periods must be accounted for.  
A typical hypercare period may be somewhere between three and four weeks, with a 
gradual taper from around the clock onsite coverage to a remote as -needed model.  ○
Not only should the customer -facing onsite support resources be allocated, but also offsite 
resources who can help aid the support team in the resolution of issues, implementation of 
code fixes or enhancements, and other matters.  ○•
Concerning a multi -site deployment, in theory the first site to be deployed should align with 
development of a global template that encompasses a large degree of functionality that will be 
required for subsequent sites.  Thereafter, subsequent site implementations should be shorter in 
duration, largely requiring delta functionality implementation that is subsequently rolled into the 
global template, master data definition / import, and deployment activities.  •

Deployment Roadmap Formulation
The deployment roadmap details how the solution stack is envisioned to be deployed across the area, 
site, enterprise based on the overall scope of the initiative.  This plan helps to establish the required 
implementation project phases upon which the quotation effort can be based.  As a result, this activity 
naturally progresses to the Spend Allocation Phase.  
There is no prescribed 'one size fits all' methodology for solution deployment, as a variety of factors 
both internal to the selected solution stack and external to the initiative must be considered.  However, 
this document will help to highlight key decision points that can shape the deployment vision.  
A goal at this stage is to keep the roadmap simple in nature so that it can be easily understood by 
various stakeholders within the customer organization.  It is not meant to be a detailed project schedule 
containing all tasks and dependencies.  Rather, it is used to establish consensus and foster discussion 
concerning when various process scenarios will be realized, and when supporting efforts must be 
executed to ensure success.  
Time Horizons:
Often, a solution roadmap is thought of in terms of short -, mid -, and long -term time horizons.  
Short -term scope items are the most thoroughly defined and can usually be quoted in a fixed -price or 
time & materials manner.  Short -term items support platform establishment and 'quick -wins' to anchor 
the solution, begin to deliver value, and lay the foundation for longer -term initiative.  Short -term scope 
items have a clear ROI in terms of replacement of legacy systems and/or tangible ROI with a reasonable 
payback period.  
Mid-term scope items may be more complex in nature with longer lead times and value propositions 
that are less clear.  They likely require prerequisite aspects of the solution to be established and adopted 
before they can be implemented.  They may have longer development lead times due to custom 
development requirements (extension of a platform or custom solution development).  The ROI payback 
period of these items may be longer in duration.  Mid -term scope items may only be able to be quoted 
in a budgetary manner with a +/ -range due to requirement unclarity or unknown dependencies.  
Long -term scope items are the most complex in nature and/or have the longest lead times.  The value 
proposition of these items may be difficult to define but extremely impactful if achieved.  These items 
are often considered 'stretch goals' utilizing advanced technological concepts that may not yet be fully 
accessible (new features not yet incorporated into a platform, technology not yet commercially available 
at a reasonable cost, etc.).  Examples of long -term scope items may include leveraging of AI 
technologies, incorporation of advanced functionality such as vision systems, robotics, etc., digital twin 
simulation, virtual reality, and other technologies.  
The long term time horizon helps to establish a vision that can help build momentum for the building 
blocks required to achieve such a state.  These items typically can only be quoted by providing a rough 
order of magnitude (ROM) estimate establishing a rough budgetary ballpark.  (Published) MES RIS 102.9 -Deployment Roadmap
