Mid-and long -term scope items can be fluid in nature as the initiative progresses.  Often, unforeseen 
value is provided in early phases that negates the need for the envisioned functionality, or new priorities 
come to light that were not thought of at the time of roadmap development.  As a result, the roadmap 
should be revisited periodically throughout the initiative, and should be a review topic during periodic 
governance reviews.  
Internal Dependencies:
The roadmap must allocate proper time to designing, implementing, testing, and deploying the 
functionality in question.  A detailed schedule is not required to determine this, but high -level timing 
estimates will need to be developed based upon the complexity of the envisioned scope items.  
Prerequisite tasks will need to be considered.  It may not be possible to provide accurate OEE 
visualizations until schedule execution functionality is deployed, so that target production counts and 
product information is known for the run for example.  Automating quality procedures may require 
development of an external interface to quality instrumentation.  
Hardware lead times may also be a factor.  This includes servers, scanners, tablets, sensors, vision 
systems, etc.  
External Dependencies:
The digitalization roadmap cannot be considered in isolation -external dependencies must be factored 
into the plan.  For example, often MES and ERP initiatives are executed in parallel.  The ERP schedule 
must align to the MES schedule so that needed ERP functions are available when testing / deploying the 
MES, and vice versa.  This also applies to any other parallel initiatives (control system upgrades, quality 
system deployment, etc.).  
Customer team availability should also be considered.  If the customer has a small support team or 
needs time to scale the team, this could impact the deployment timeline.  Other external activities such 
as training time may also impact the timeline.  
Decoupling the Magnitude of Change:
A useful strategy when formulating a digitalization roadmap is decoupling large system deployments to 
reduce the amount of change that must be managed by operations at one time, as well as reduce the 
size of the team that will be required to support deployment and hypercare activities.  In some instances 
employing these strategies may increase the scope of the implementation or require later re -work, but 
this is outweighed by the change management benefits.  
An example of deploying this strategy is employing a gradual deployment model where functionality is 
deployed to subsets of the site footprint sequentially.  For example, the solution may be deployed to the 
batching area first, then the packaging area.  Or the solution could be deployed across production lines 
in a staggered manner.  However, care must be taken to ensure that these sorts of methodologies do 
not require operators, supervisors, etc. to 'bounce' between systems as they move from line to line or 
area to area, which could cause undue confusion and lead to mistakes being made.  
Another strategy involves gradual deployment of functionality.  Production management may be 
deployed first, then quality, then efficiency for example.  This strategy can be especially beneficial if for 
example the enterprise relies upon delineated 'point solutions' that can be gradually decommissioned.  
For example, the production execution functionality could be deployed while the customer continues to 
leverage a legacy quality system, then eventually that quality system be replaced by a deployed module 
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 72    
leverage a legacy quality system, then eventually that quality system be replaced by a deployed module 
within the MES platform.  
Yet another strategy with integrated MES and ERP deployments is to decouple the MES deployment 
from the ERP deployment.  For example, it may be possible to extend the MES to communicate with 
legacy ERP systems, deploy the MES first and anchor it, then deploy the ERP and cut over the MES 
interfaces.  This strategy will require coordination with other customer teams to ensure such a model is 
achievable, and may require extra work to create additional interfaces to legacy systems, but can have 
huge benefits in terms of site acceptance.  
Greenfield Deployment Considerations:
A greenfield deployment presents unique challenges to roadmap formulation, as there will typically be a 
base level of functionality that must be delivered to support the startup of the facility.  It may not be 
possible to deliver the full scope of the solution on day 1 due to timing constraints, so functionality may 
need to be prioritized based on immediate vs. longer -term business impact.  In these scenarios, the 
hierarchy of required functions often aligns to the following:
Work instructions and procedures: New employees and new equipment will require proper work 
instructions / workflows to be established early so that plant processes are quickly learned and 
understood.  With a greenfield deployment, procedures may change frequently so it is important 
to make this functionality data -driven in nature with the ability to be quickly updated and re -
deployed.  -
Production: functions supporting the execution of the production schedule, tracking of order 
progress, materials used (genealogy), and finished goods output.  This information may be 
received from and provided to the ERP layer to support customer order tracking and material 
requirements planning (MRP) activities.  -
Quality: functions supporting the confirmation of product quality, including sample and test 
execution, non -conformance workflows, and product disposition.  There may be manual processes 
that can be enacted in the short term to track quality as a stop -gap, but digitalization of this 
functionality will still be a high -priority.  In regulated industries such as life sciences, quality may 
actually be a higher -priority than production tracking.  -
Efficiency: functions supporting efficiency tracking and reporting, such as equipment utilization, 
overall equipment effectiveness (OEE), etc.  Greenfield plants usually must be well established and 
a basis of data captured before meaningful efficiency insights can be acted upon.  -
Maintenance Optimization: A new facility with new equipment will generally perform in a more 
reliable manner, reducing the need for maintenance management and maintenance process 
optimization in the short term.  -
Energy Management: A new facility with new equipment will likely utilize energy more efficiently 
than legacy sites.  As a result, insights from energy utilization information may not be as important 
in the short term.  -

Enterprise Multiple Site Sequencing:
There are certain factors to balance when defining a multi -site deployment roadmap.  Customers will 
often want our recommendation as to the sequence in which site deployments should occur.  The pros 
and cons of deploying to certain sites early or late in the roadmap should be captured.  Some factors for 
consideration include the following:
Some sites are more open/tolerant to change than others.  This can be due to the site culture, 
management, workforce age, history of the site, location, and other factors.  It may be beneficial 
to deploy to sites more open to change first, to gain momentum, secure quicker ROI, and groom 
advocates for the solution that can help win over more reluctant sites.  -
Some sites are more ready for the solution than others.  Sites possessing modern infrastructure 
and control system automation may more easily be able to support deployment of the solution 
without costly infrastructure / controls upgrades.  It may be beneficial to deploy to these sites first 
while in parallel performing upgrades to less modern facilities.  
However, this should be balanced with the fact that more ROI may be achievable in less 
modern sites.  ○-
Smaller sites may support faster deployments with less overall risk to the organization.  
Deployment to smaller sites early in the roadmap can build momentum and prove out solution 
functionality with minimal negative impact.  However, the ROI for small site deployments may not 
be as great as that for larger sites, so these two factors should be balanced.  It may make sense to 
deploy to a small site, and then a large site to take advantage of both derisking and ROI 
attainment factors early in the roadmap.    -
It may be beneficial to deploy to sites near an established RoviSys office and/or customer HQ early 
in the roadmap.  Sites early in the deployment roadmap will likely require a larger support 
structure, so the ability for RoviSys and customer resources to travel to the site expediently could 
pay dividends. -
Sites with similar equipment and/or work processes could be clustered together to support a 
more aggressive deployment schedule.  For example, all of the type 'A' plants could be deployed 
sequentially while providing time to develop functionality for all the type 'B' plants as these 
deployments progress.  -
Some sites may have a stronger need for the solution than others.  Maybe a given site has a legacy 
system that is no longer maintainable or is utilizing inefficient paper -based processes.  Or, the site 
manufactures a high -cost product with a high -scrap rate than needs to be lowered.  Sites yielding 
the greatest potential for ROI should be considered early in the roadmap to help justify the 
initiative.  -

Executive Summary
The executive summary presentation distills the activities, key findings, and recommendations into a 
format that can be digested by broader customer stakeholders including an executive leadership team 
or steering committee.  It should present a compelling plan that highlights the benefits of the initiative, 
roadmap, and keys to success.  
Presentation Components:
The following are the topics typical of an executive summary presentation
Agenda:
The agenda should be presented at the beginning of the presentation so that the group at hand 
understands what will be covered during the discussion.  
Introduction:
Key RoviSys assessment team members, their roles, and credentials should be captured and presented.  
RoviSys Background:
Customer stakeholders unfamiliar with RoviSys will likely benefit from a brief overview of our size, 
locations, and capabilities.  This introduction should be quick and to the point, allowing for ample time 
to cover the logistics and findings within the assessment itself.  
DxArchitecture Activity Overview:
This section should present an overview of the assessment activities and overall timeline involved.
Key Individuals and Sites:
This section should present the key individuals from which information was solicited or who reviewed 
and approved various aspects of the assessment findings.  In the case of a global enterprise -centric 
assessment, the representative site(s) of focus and reasons for selection of those sites as focuses should 
be discussed.  
Capabilities of Focus:
Summarization of a standard capability map and presentation of the capabilities of focus is useful to lay 
the foundation for the focus of the assessment, including functional capabilities in scope and out of 
scope.  
Key Findings:
The customer stakeholders for whom the presented is targeted likely understands the manufacturing 
and associated operational processes at a high -level.  However, key findings should be summarized, 
including gaps, concerns, and challenges pertaining to current operational workflows.  
Business Process Scenario Summary:

Procedure Overview
The DxExecution Procedure outlines our approach for executing digital transformation projects. Its 
primary goal is to streamline project execution, thereby increasing our ability to consistently deliver 
high -quality results. By seamlessly blending flexibility with structure, DxExecution enables us to adapt to 
changes while maintaining defined milestones, budgets, and schedules. Our commitment to 
transparency and regular communication ensures that every stage of the project is successful and that 
end users receive the tools they need to work more effectively.
The DxExecution RAP consists of three key phases:
Mobilization:
This initial phase lays the foundation for the project. During Mobilization, we develop a detailed 
work breakdown structure and compile a comprehensive project backlog. This backlog prioritizes 
features and user stories, which are essential for defining future sprints.1.
Planning:
In the Planning phase, the project backlog is thoroughly evaluated. The team then identifies and 
organizes the components of each sprint, ensuring that every user story is well -defined and that 
acceptance criteria are in place for successful implementation.2.
Execution:
During the Execution phase, the development team works on the selected tasks from the sprint 
backlog to meet the defined goals. Although the Planning and Execution phases are presented 
sequentially, they are in practice iterative processes that continue until the entire project scope is 
addressed.3.

DxSustainment
The goal of the DxSustainment effort is to ensure that the customer's technology investment remains 
healthy and viable.  A solution that is out -of-date, hard to support, buggy, or slow -performing will be 
poorly received by the system's user base, and is more likely to be poorly used or abandoned.  The 
DxSustainment effort applies both to systems implemented and deployed by RoviSys and systems 
deployed by others.  In the latter case, the customer may have become frustrated by the previous 
vendor's lack of ongoing support and reached out to RoviSys to help salvage the system so that the 
customer can recoup their technology investment.  
In the case of a system installed by RoviSys, we may be able to draw upon the experience of the project 
team who implemented the system, as well as archived source code, configuration, and documentation.  
In the case of a system installed by others, we will need to quickly triage the system state.  In both cases, 
detailed planning and execution of the sustainment strategy is key to resolving ongoing issues and 
ensuring proactive steps are taken to maintain system value.  
The following features are captured as part of our DxSustainment productized services offering:
System Evaluation:
The system evaluation effort allows the team to gather information concerning the system that will be 
leveraged to formulate a sustainment strategy.  Infrastructure, system versions, log files, server 
resources, and other metrics will be captured and analyzed.  
Knowledge Transfer:
Knowledge transfer allows RoviSys to gain information from various user roles concerning their usage of 
the system, and specific challenges and pain points.  This may include bugs that must be worked around, 
ideas for enhancements, issues accessing the system, and performance concerns.
Additional knowledge transfer may also be required between the current RoviSys project support team 
and new team members who may be brought into the project engagement in a support capability.  This 
includes not only knowledge transfer concerning the system software platform, but also nuances 
concerning the implementation and common support issues.  
Support Desk Establishment:
The support desk provides a means for the customer to submit a support incident (such as an issue or 
enhancement) and provides notification to the support team of this submittal.  The support desk also 
facilitates the ability to track issues and enhancements reported by the customer, including resolution 
status, individual assigned as responsible for the resolution of the support incident, and a trail of 
correspondence that can be consulted should future similar issues arise.  
Knowledge Base Creation:
A knowledge base concerning previous project issues and resolutions greatly aids the project team by 
reducing duplication of troubleshooting efforts.  Common support issues, including abnormal (Published) MES RAP 107 -DxSustainment

When quoting a DxSustainment extended support agreement for an MES project, it is crucial to 
structure the agreement to include necessary activities, define clear support tiers, and establish key 
assumptions that will impact service delivery. A well -defined agreement ensures that both RoviSys and 
the customer have a clear understanding of expectations, available resources, and the cost structure for 
ongoing support.
Key Activities to be Quoted in an MES Extended Support Agreement:
Note that the number of hours allocated to each key activity should be scaled based on the scope, size, 
and age of the system being supported. Additionally, if the agreement encompasses multiple sites with 
substantial differences, the activity durations must be scaled according to the number of sites.
1. Project Management
Effective project management is essential for ensuring the smooth execution of support activities. The 
proposal should include time allocation for:
Coordination of support tasks•
Scheduling and tracking of activities•
Regular status meetings with stakeholders•

ensures that the support team has the necessary insights into the MES implementation, reducing 
resolution time for future issues. The proposal should include quoting for the following activities:

Training on customizations and specific configurations•
Walkthroughs of application processes•

beginning of the support engagement by a lead or architect -level resource. This review provides:

Validation of system parameters and configurations•
Identification of potential technical debt that may affect supportability•
Time should be allocated in the proposal for this review to ensure efficient future support.

Assess system performance and stability•
Identify known issues and their current resolutions•
Confirm the availability of logs, monitoring tools, and documentation•

support phase.

Periodic Health Audit
A periodic health audit allows RoviSys to verify the overall well -being of the customer's digitalization 
stack, and recommend actions to ensure system performance, reliability, and robustness.  The health 
audit must follow a pre -defined checklist to ensure that no required steps are missed.  This checklist 
should be executed by an assigned DxSustainment project team member and archived in a project 
repository as completed.  
The initial audit (or any audit involving a new auditor who is brought onto the DxSustainment 
engagement) should be overseen by the technical lead to ensure that the auditor properly completes 
the audit checklist steps.  
The checklist will be formulated by the project technical lead (or a designee) and tailored specifically to 
the project, including the software systems in place, software hosting model (on -premises vs. cloud), 
and application functionality.  The checklist must be very specific in nature, such that a resource 
unfamiliar with the overall build and architecture of the solution could execute it if required.  This 
includes calling out specific server names, disks utilized, SQL server locations, log file locations, 
application service / module names, and other critical information to facilitate expedient and complete 
completion of the checklist.  
Frequency:
An audit frequency should be established that balances cost with the risk to the system should an 
unnoticed error go undetected.  A mission critical system responsible for production execution should 
generally be audited more frequently than a passive reporting system.  A monthly audit is often a 
recommended cadence.

Root Cause Resolution:
In cases where a potential issue is discovered, particularly concerning matters of resource utilization, the 
RoviSys auditor must examine the root cause of the issue rather than recommend a resolution that 
simply masks the issue.  As a common example, in the cases of poor system performance or disk 
utilization approaching 100%, RoviSys may recommend a system resource increase (addition of CPU 
cores, RAM, or hard disk to the server).  However, there may be an underlying issue, such as a repetitive 
error being generated by the system, SQL fragmentation, data collection triggered too frequently, etc.  
In these cases the underlying cause of the issue must be resolved to avoid unnecessary system resource 
cost or the potential that the issue becomes worse over time.

Infrastructure Refresh
Over the lifecycle of an MES application, it may be necessary to refresh on -premises infrastructure due 
to normal system aging and corresponding software advancement.  Refreshing infrastructure is a 
complex process with multiple considerations. This article outlines key factors to include in an MES 
infrastructure refresh..  
The customer's IT organization must formulate and approve a plan detailing the activities involved in the 
infrastructure refresh. 
This plan must first consider formulation of an architecture to present the future state infrastructure.  
Considerations in this architecture include the following:
Will the infrastructure hosting the MES platform remain on -premises or is a cloud migration 
planned?  Migration to the cloud requires confirmation of software support, network 
implementation to ensure data movement between on -premises and cloud, and the potential for 
edge devices to aid in bridging data transfer to/from cloud -hosted applications.  -
Server sizing, including CPU, RAM, hard disk, etc.:  Servers should be sized based on both current 
and future need, considering increased data volume and additional system demands should the 
MES platform be upgraded.  
Application stacks are often deployed to virtual infrastructure, enabling dynamic allocation 
of resources when needed.  However, IT organizations often limit resource allocation for 
individual applications and take a conservative approach.  It is important to express the 
recommended application requirements to ensure no impact to the production 
environment after the refresh.  ○-
Server OS and software versioning: It must be confirmed that the versions of the various 
components in the digitalization software stack are compatible with the operating system and 
associated software (such as SQL server, web server, frameworks (such as .NET, python, 
JavaScript, etc.) to be deployed to the refreshed infrastructure.  It may be necessary to also 
consider a technology upgrade should there be a desire to upgrade to an operating system or SQL 
version that is incompatible with the current version of the MES or other digitalization software 
components.  -
Custom integrations and APIs, including scripts, third -party tools, and middleware, must be 
reviewed for compatibility with the upgraded infrastructure.  Any changes to these integrations 
required must be documented in the architecture and tested as part of the upgrade plan.  -
High availability and Redundancy: an infrastructure refresh is a good time to consider 
improvements to the infrastructure to improve reliability and redundancy.  This includes failover 
mechanisms such as clustered servers, load balancers, and RAID storage.  -
Cybersecurity compliance: deployment of upgraded firewalls, endpoint protection, and security 
appliances should all be considered to mitigate cyber security risks.
This deployment may require configuration to ensure the digitalization platforms continue 
to function properly.  For example, ports leveraged by the application may need to be 
opened or certain point to point communication exceptions be configured to ensure data 
flows to/from external application and devices.  ○
Incorporation of enhanced security protections, such as multi -factor authentication (MFA) 
should also be considered.  ○-
Many digitalization platforms are beginning to move to a containerized environment.  
Containerization is advantageous in that it permits more rapid deployment and many better -(Published) MES RIS 107.8 -Infrastructure Refresh

Containerization is advantageous in that it permits more rapid deployment and many better 
support redundancy, but may present unique architectural constraints such as requirement for a 
specific OS and installation of the container hosting application.  Should containerization be 
supported, migration to a containerized environment must be factored into the architecture and 
migration plan.  
The plan must then consider the migration steps.  As part of migration, the digitalization software stack 
may need to be transitioned from the existing to new infrastructure.  Depending on the magnitude of 
the refresh, this may entail application re -installation, database migration, configuration and code re -
deployment, and other factors.  The plan should look to minimize both risk and system downtime 
wherever possible.  
Considerations to be documented as part of the migration plan include:
Benchmark key performance indicators before and after the refresh, such as database query 
times, application latency, and server resource utilization, to ensure no performance degradation 
and ideally a performance improvement that helps to justify the refresh effort.  -
A contingency strategy must be incorporated to ensure any production disruption is minimized.  A 
common aspect of such strategy is maintaining the legacy infrastructure throughout the process 
so that as a contingency production can fall back to the existing infrastructure if required.  
Usage of paper -based records or other manual contingencies may also factor into the 
infrastructure refresh plan.  This data will need to be synchronized post -cutover and a plan 
for doing so, including required roles and resources, must be established.  ○-
Will server names change or remain the same?  A change to server names may require 
configuration changes within the MES, Historian, and/or other middleware components.  Testing 
should be conducted to confirm that there are no hardcoded server names within the 
code/configuration or missed server name references.  -
Can the new servers be stood up and application installation occur prior to the cutover, reducing 
the cutover time?  Doing this may require the new servers to be on an isolated network or certain 
data conduits to be disabled so that there are not conflicts with the production environments.  
Data migration likely cannot occur until the actual cutover.  In some cases, a majority of the 
data may be able to be migrated, and then a partial migration of data captured in 
production subsequent to the bulk migration may be feasible, but this is generally not 
supported by most MES applications.  As a result, customized tools may need to be 
developed to facilitate this if minimization of downtime is of sufficient importance to justify 
this.  More commonly, the database will need to be migrated in its entirety during the 
cutover and restored to the new environment, then any needed configuration changes (such 
as server renames) made.  ○
An infrastructure refresh is an ideal opportunity to purge non -critical data according to an 
established retention policy.  This will ensure both data retention compliance as well as 
ensure that the database is as small as possible, increasing the efficiency of the database 
migration.  
It may be necessary to shrink the database and associated data files to realize the size 
reduction.  ▪
This is also a good time to ensure that periodic database maintenance is performed 
prior to the refresh, such as addressing index fragmentation.  ▪○-
Capture of key backup steps, including database backups, configuration backups, code backups, 
and environment snapshots to ensure contingency plans can be executed should they be required.  -
Reestablishment of any data conduits that may have been disabled to prevent accidental 
interference with production data conduits.  -
Timing of when the refresh will take place.  It may be feasible to perform the upgrade during a 
time in which the plant is down (not scheduled, holiday, shift change, etc.) or when data load is 
minimized (night shift for example).  -
Communication plan to inform operations of any system outages, needed workarounds (such as -

Communication plan to inform operations of any system outages, needed workarounds (such as 
paper -based data capture) and expected durations.  -
Coordination channels during the infrastructure refresh.  An onsite presence may be required, or 
an open web conference call established to ensure proper communications between the various 
teams.  A chain -of-command hierarchy may be needed to ensure that should quick decisions need 
to be made approvals can be granted.  -
Manage licensing migration, whether transferring existing licenses or acquiring new ones from 
vendors.
Some platform vendors leverage licensing dependent on the specific hardware (such as MAC 
address or physical server keys), requiring a license refresh from the vendor prior to 
enablement of the new environment.  ○
Licensing for ancillary components, such as OPC servers or other middleware, must also be 
considered.  ○-
Redirection of client workstations, tablets, etc. to the new infrastructure, particularly in the event 
that there is a server name change or migration from on -premises to containerized or cloud 
infrastructure.  -
Testing the various digitalization applications on the upgraded infrastructure in a quarantined 
manner prior to the upgrade.  It is recommended to setup the new infrastructure and install the 
applications, taking care to isolate them from production systems and data connections, to 
confirm the upgrade steps and verify proper application function prior to the cutover.  -
A system outage associated with the refresh may cause inaccurate OEE / performance metrics.  
Manual corrections may be required to ensure this impact is not factored into periodic 
performance reporting.  -
There may be an opportunity to introduce or leverage automated test scripts to quickly ensure 
system integrity post -refresh without extensive manual testing steps.  When considering 
implementation of such test scripts, areas with the greatest probability of impact post -refresh 
should be considered, such modules that may be sensitive to data conduit interruption, server 
name changes, or other similar aspects.  -
Enhanced system logging may need to be enabled during the refresh process to allow for closer 
monitoring of potential errors or issues.  Ensure that any enhanced tracking that was enabled is 
disabled after normal operation is confirmed, to prevent performance impact or excessive system 
resource consumption by logging activities.  -
Any system documentation that must be changed must be identified and edited as part of the 
refresh activities. -
Disaster recovery testing should be planned to ensure backup restoration and failover 
mechanisms work as expected.  -
After the refresh, increased attention must be given to the application and associated infrastructure, 
allocating support time and resources to respond to any issues.  In particular, the following factors 
should be closely monitored:
Server performance, including CPU, RAM, and hard disk usage-
Inability of certain clients to connect-
Any reports of system slowness, screens or functions that will not execute, or system bugs-
Failed data transactions, or external system communication errors (for example to -from the ERP, 
shop floor equipment, instrumentation, etc.)-
After the upgrade, document lessons learned and improvement opportunities to streamline future 
infrastructure refreshes, capturing any pain points or strategies employed to ensure that any future 
infrastructure refreshes are conducted as smoothly as possible.

System Impact Notifications and Updates
This procedure establishes a structured process for notifying shop floor personnel about changes, 
upgrades, or enhancements to digitalization applications and/or infrastructure. This procedure ensures 
that all affected personnel are informed about the change, potential impacts, workarounds, and 
contingency plans to maintain operational continuity.  While proper communication is ultimately the 
customer's responsibility, the customer may be unfamiliar with such strategies and rely upon RoviSys to 
aid in proper execution of a system impact notification and update plan.  
This procedure applies to all planned digitalization application or infrastructure change s, including but 
not limited to:
System upgrades and migrations•
Software patches and enhancements•
Server, database, and network changes•
Integration updates with ERP, SCADA, and shop floor equipment•
Security and compliance updates affecting user access•
The following roles and responsibilities must be involved in the notification process:
IT / OT Departments: Responsible for planning, executing, and communicating changes •
Operations / Production Managers: Ensure shop floor personnel understand the impact and 
workarounds•

Root Cause Analysis
Performing a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) for an MES (Manufacturing Execution System) application issue 
requires a structured approach to identifying and resolving the problem effectively. While the specific 
troubleshooting steps depend greatly on the MES platform, data connections, and infrastructure, the 
following are general strategies:
1. Define the Problem Clearly
Gather details on what the issue is, when it started, who reported it, and how it affects 
operations.•
Categorize the issue (e.g., performance degradation, incorrect data, connectivity issues, UI errors).•
2. Reproduce & Validate the Issue
Check if the issue is consistent or intermittent.•
Identify the affected modules, transactions, or processes.•
Determine whether it occurs in production, test, or both environments.•
3. Collect and Analyze Logs & System Data
Check MES application logs for errors or warnings.•
Review database logs for slow queries, deadlocks, or data inconsistencies.•
Utilize a database query profiling tool (such as SQL Server Profiler) to analyze long -running queries •
Monitor server performance (CPU, memory, disk I/O).•
Examine network logs for latency or packet loss.•
Check browser console logs (for web -based MES systems). •
4. Isolate Contributing Factors
Recent software updates or configuration changes.•
Database schema modifications or incorrect data inputs.•
External system integrations (ERP, SCADA, IoT).•
User actions that may trigger the issue.•
System resource constraints or hardware failures.•
5. Use the "5 Whys" or Fishbone Diagram
Apply the 5 Whys method to drill down into the root cause.•
Use a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram to categorize possible causes (software, hardware, network, 
process, user actions).•
6. Test Hypotheses & Validate the Root Cause
Replicate the issue in a controlled test environment.•
Apply temporary fixes (rollback changes, restart services, etc.).•
Use debugging tools to trace errors and bottlenecks.•
7. Implement & Verify the Fix
Deploy a fix in a staging environment before production.•
Ensure that the solution does not create new issues.•
Monitor system behavior post -fix. •(Published) MES RIS 107.10 -Root Cause Analysis

8. Prevent Recurrence
Implement automated monitoring for similar failures.•
Improve error handling & logging.•
Update documentation with RCA findings.•
Train users or update SOPs if needed.•
While MES troubleshooting varies by platform, infrastructure, and integrations, these general strategies 
provide a structured approach to identifying and resolving issues efficiently.
Usage of 5 Whys Strategy:
The 5 Whys is a root cause analysis (RCA) technique used to identify the underlying cause of a problem 
by repeatedly asking "Why?" until the fundamental issue is uncovered. It was developed as part of 
Toyota's Lean Manufacturing System but is widely used in other areas, including MES troubleshooting.
How to Perform the 5 Whys Analysis (example):
State the Problem Clearly
Example: "Production reports in the MES are showing incorrect data."○1.
Ask ‘Why?’ (First Level)
Why is the production report incorrect?
→ Because the MES is pulling incorrect values from the database.○2.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Second Level)
Why is the MES pulling incorrect values?
→ Because the database has duplicate and outdated records.○3.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Third Level)
Why does the database have duplicate and outdated records?
→ Because the data synchronization process failed.○4.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Fourth Level)
Why did the data synchronization process fail?
→ Because a scheduled job responsible for syncing data was not executed.○5.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Fifth Level -Root Cause)
Why was the scheduled job not executed?
→ Because the job scheduler crashed due to a lack of memory on the server.○6.
Root Cause Identified:
The MES reporting issue originated from insufficient server memory, leading to job failures and, 
eventually, incorrect production reports.•
Usage of a Fishbone Diagram to Perform Systematic Evaluation:
A Fishbone Diagram, also known as an Ishikawa Diagram or Cause -and-Effect Diagram, is a tool used to 
identify the root causes of a problem systematically. It allows the troubleshooter to visually maps out 
potential factors contributing to an issue, organizing them into major categories.
Structure of a Fishbone Diagram:
The "head" of the fish represents the problem statement (effect).•
The "spine" is the main horizontal line extending from the head.•
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 134    
The "spine" is the main horizontal line extending from the head.•
Major categories (causes) branch off the spine as bones.•
Sub-causes are further detailed under each category. •
Common Categories in MES Troubleshooting:
For MES troubleshooting, common cause categories may include:
Software –Bugs, application crashes, configuration errors. 1.
Hardware –Server failures, disk I/O, memory issues. 2.
Database –Slow queries, data corruption, connection timeouts. 3.
Network –Latency, firewall issues, dropped packets. 4.
User Actions –Incorrect input, unauthorized access, training gaps. 5.
External Systems –ERP, SCADA, IoT device failures, API issues. 6.

Hardware: Database server running low on disk space•
Database: Data synchronization failure•
Network: High latency between MES and SCADA•
User Actions: Incorrect manual data entry•
External Systems: ERP sending duplicate data records•
Of increased benefit is once formulated, a created fishbone diagram can be saved to the knowledge 
base established for the platform, shortcutting future potential troubleshooting efforts.  
Increasing Root Cause Analysis Effectiveness:
As part of the DxSustainment offering, RoviSys should aid the customer in establishing practices that will 
aid in future root cause analysis.  Such practices include the following:
Maintain detailed version control of MES configurations and database changes•
Ensure all deployed updates have a rollback procedure documented in case a recent update 
introduces issues•
Ensure that development and sandbox / staging environments are leveraged to replicate 
production scenarios•
Establish application performance monitoring (APM) tools for real -time system insights and 
ensure notifications are configured to key individuals should issues be detected by these tools•
Leveraging infrastructure refresh and technology upgrade strategies, ensure that the 
infrastructure and software applications are kept reasonably up -to-date•
Evaluate the inclusion of additional logging and monitoring, particularly around risk areas such as 
external system transactions•
Capture of root cause issue and associated resolution in a searchable knowledge base•

Minor Enhancements
As part of a DxSustainment contract, performing minor enhancements can improve system 
functionality and usability without necessitating a full -scale change request (CR). However, clear 
guidelines must be in place to determine when an enhancement qualifies as a minor update rather 
than a major change requiring formal approval. Additionally, a structured approach to risk 
assessment, testing, and migration is essential to ensure system stability and maintainability.
Establishing an Enhancement Threshold:
A key aspect of MES sustainment is defining what constitutes a minor enhancement versus a 
significant change requiring a formal change request (CR). A well -defined threshold should consider 
factors such as:
Impact on existing functionality –Minor enhancements should not disrupt critical processes or 
introduce significant workflow changes.•
Complexity and effort required –Small configuration changes, UI tweaks, and minor 
automation improvements generally fall within sustainment scope, while extensive logic 
modifications may require a CR.•
Risk level –The enhancement should not introduce potential vulnerabilities or require 
substantial regression testing across the system.•
By establishing clear criteria, MES sustainment teams can ensure that minor enhancements are 
handled efficiently while more substantial modifications undergo proper review and approval 
processes.
Risk Assessment for Minor Enhancements:
Even minor enhancements carry some level of risk, making risk assessment a crucial step before 
implementation. The risk assessment process should include:
Impact analysis –Evaluating which areas of the MES may be affected by the enhancement, 
including dependencies on external systems such as ERP or LIMS, or shop -floor equipment.•
Regression testing scope –Identifying the extent of testing required to verify that the 
enhancement does not introduce unintended consequences.•
Rollback strategy –Ensuring that changes can be reversed if issues arise during 
implementation.•
By proactively assessing risks, sustainment teams can prevent disruptions and ensure a seamless 
transition from development to production.
Prerequisites for Implementing Minor Enhancements:
Before making any MES enhancement, several prerequisites should be met to maintain system 
integrity and minimize risks:
Development -Test -Production Environment –A structured environment for deploying changes 
is essential. All enhancements should be developed and tested in a dedicated development 
environment before being validated in a test environment and finally deployed to production.1.
Source Code and Configuration Management –The latest version of all MES configurations, 2.(Published) MES RIS 107.11 -Minor Enhancements

Change Documentation –Even for minor enhancements, maintaining documentation of the

Automated Testing Where Possible –Automating regression tests can improve validation 
efficiency and reduce the risk of unintended consequences.•
Monitoring Post -Deployment –Implementing monitoring mechanisms to track system 
behavior after deployment can help quickly identify and address any unexpected issues.•

Vendor Support Engagement
As an independent systems integrator, we are uniquely positioned to act as a liaison between our 
customers and their vendors. Our role is to bridge communication gaps, ensure smooth coordination of 
support activities, and advise on best practices for system maintenance and upgrades. This document 
outlines the procedures we should follow to assist our customers in managing vendor relationships, 
troubleshooting application support issues, and planning for infrastructure refreshes and updates.
RoviSys can provide more effective support when we have an established relationship with a prioritized 
vendor. If we are unfamiliar with a vendor or lack an existing relationship, we may still assist, but our 
effectiveness may be limited. Customers should be made aware of this potential limitation.
Proposal Assumptions:
As part of the DxSustainment contract establishment, roles and responsibilities should be clearly 
delineated.  RoviSys should be positioned in an assist role, but ultimately the vendor must be positioned 
as responsible for the proper function of their software platform.  
Additionally, any prerequisites to be established to ensure RoviSys access to vendor support must be 
clearly stated in the assumptions.  For example, the customer may be required to ensure they maintain 
a support contract with the vendor, maintain a current supported version of the software, and devote 
recommended server resources to the application per the vendor's guidelines.  Customers often assume 
that having a support contract with RoviSys eliminates the need for a separate vendor support contract, 
but this is incorrect.  
Assumptions must also be clearly stated in the proposal around response times / SLAs.  RoviSys cannot 
be expected to meet a certain response or resolution time in the event that an issue requires vendor 
engagement, as RoviSys has little control over the timing of the vendor response.  This must be clarified 
in the proposal to minimize the risk to RoviSys.  
Vendor Support Engagement Execution:
The following are ways in which RoviSys can aid in vendor engagement that should be considered 
throughout the duration of our DxSustainment contract:
Establishing Vendor Contact Points
Maintain an up -to-date database of customer vendors, including contact persons, escalation 
paths, and support processes•
Ensure that customers are aware of the appropriate channels for contacting vendors•
Act as a primary or secondary point of contact for vendor communications when required by the 
customer•
Streamlining Issue Reporting
Triage issues by distinguishing:
Platform -related issues requiring vendor engagement ○
Application or customization issues that the vendor cannot resolve○
Training -related concerns that can be handled internally•(Published) MES RIS 107.12 -Vendor Support Engagement

Act as a trusted advisor to help customers navigate technological advancements and strategic

Vendor Support Watchouts:
As the customer's trusted advisor, RoviSys can help guard against unrealistic vendor expectations or 
requests.  Vendor support resources often lack perspective concerning management of their platform in 
a production environment, leading to asks that may not be practical.  These include the following:
A vendor may request a customer deploy a patch or upgrade to the latest version of the software 
as an initial step before providing support.  This may be impractical in a production environment 
due to resulting system downtime or risk of outage should a problem arise.  RoviSys can help plan 
for such an update, or independently evaluate if the request makes sense.  The request may be 
unreasonable if the customer is running a supported version of the software, even if the customer 
is not running the latest revision.  •
A vendor may request a database backup without realizing that it may be too large to transmit 
efficiently or contain proprietary information that cannot be shared with a third party.  RoviSys 
can help communicate this impracticality to the vendor, as well as scrub the database or export 
configuration relevant to issue troubleshooting.  •

Summary    
This document outlines travel, and associated expenses, related to RoviSys  employees traveling to RoviSys  offices.  
 
Travel Approval  Requirements  
In all cases, inter-office travel must be approved prior to booking or engaging in any travel  or expenses. Travel  
associated with project activities should be approved by the RoviSys  assigned PM or RM; whereas  travel not  
associated with project activities should be approved by the Employee’s GM or Director.  
 
The travel approver shall work with the employee to designate/approve all Lodging, Meals, Rental Car or Personal  
Vehicle Mileage, and Airline options used during Inter-Office travel.  
 
Travel durations of more than 5 days, or 10+ days in a 30-day period , requires preemptive approval by both a RM o
GM and a Director. Travel that extends beyond 30 days  should align with the policies outlined in the Extended Inter
Office Travel section of this document.  
 
Exceptions to stated  policies require review and approval by the project RM, the employee’s GM, or the employee’
Director.  
 
Inter-Office Travel  
All employees  have a designated “ Office Location ” in UKG  which  defines the RoviSys  office which the employee  
reports to .  For designated “Remote Employees ”, this “O ffice Location” is assigned as “Remote” in UKG . 
 
Travel to/from your RoviSys  designated  “Office  Location ” is generally not  eligible for reimbursement .   
 
Travel and expenses to a RoviSys  office, which is not designated  as your “Office  Location ” (this also includes  
employees with a “Remote” designation traveling to any RoviSys  office)  shall be handled as defined in this sub-
RAP 306.08, RAP 306 , and any other applicable sub-RAPs to RAP 306.  
 
Expenses Policy  
All expenses associated with inter-office travel should be submitted  using the RoviSys  Expenses Application.  
 
Expenses for inter-office travel associated with customer project work should be expensed to  the appropriate  
customer  project (s); the PM/RM will determine  if the expenses are able to be invoiced to the customer or not.  
 
Expenses unrelated to project work (e.g., travelling to a RoviSys  office for a company event such as RAC or non-
project related training) are to be expensed to one (or more) divisional Admin project(s).  
 
Airline Travel, Rental Cars, Mileage (Personal Auto), and Meal & Incidental Expenses will all be regulated by the  
standard policy defined in RAP 306. Employees requiring lodging must book at an approved option  as outlined in 
Approved Lodging - Rovipedia  
 
Extended Inter-Office Travel     
Extended Inter-Office travel applies to inter-office travel that extends beyond 30 days .

written using a RoviSys  account with rent being billed directly to the company. Employees have no expense  
obligation for apartment rent. If hotels are required  during any portion  of the project, then the current expense
procedures for hotel stays shall apply.   
 
Airline Travel – Routine travel for long-term projects should be booked 2 weeks in advance to secure reasonabl
priced  tickets.  All airline travel will be expensed by each employee according to current procedures (See RAP  
306).     
 
Rental Cars  – RoviSys  employees working at RoviSys  office for  30+ days  are asked to provide  personal  
transportation at the destination office, as applicable and available. Mileage will be paid according to current  
policy for transporting the vehicle between the RoviSys  offices. Once the employee’s vehicle arrives at the non-
local office, the standard mileage policy will apply. Rental cars will be expensed and reimbursed at cost if  
needed during trips home.  
 
For example:  Joe Smith lives in Aurora, OH and must travel to Holly Springs, NC for a 5-month project. Joe  
will be reimbursed mileage to drive his vehicle from Aurora to Holly Springs . Once in NC, Joe will only be  
reimbursed for mileage between the Holly Springs  office and the customer site. Travel from Joe’s temporary
housing to the Holly Springs office is considered a local resident commute. Every other Friday, Joe flies hom
to Cleveland and uses a rental car for the weekend. The rental car can be expensed at cost per the current  
RAP.  
 
Meal & Incidental Expense  – Each employee will receive a daily per diem set according to the US General  
Services Administration’s Domestic Per Diem rates. The per diem is to cover all meal expenses associated with  
the travel. Each employee will submit  a monthly expense report for the number of days at the non-home office
Per Diem will be paid for all days (including weekends) that the employee is traveling. Per Diem rates are  
defined by the US government: https://www.gsa.gov/travel/plan-book/per-diem-rates

Fall Pr otecon
Training can be provided for each employee who might be exposed to fall hazards. The training will enable each
employee to recognize the hazards of falling and the procedures to follow to minimize these hazards. Records showing
participants, training dates and signatures of instructors must be maintained.
Re-training will be provided when there are deficiencies in training, when work practices are changed or when fall
protection equipment is modified.
Fall protection is required whenever employees are potentially exposed to falls from heights that exceed applicable
regulatory thresholds. Guard rails, safety nets, or personal or fall arrest systems should be used. Some applicable
regulatory thresholds may include:
General Industry 1910.28(b)(1)(i) - Protection for wall openings and holes. Every wall opening from which there is a drop of more than 4 feet shall be
guarded.
Construction Industry 1926.501(b)(1) - Unprotected sides and edges. Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface)
with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems,
safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.
Marine Terminals 1917.112(b)(1) - Guardrails shall be provided at locations where employees are exposed to floor or wall openings or waterside
edges, including bridges or gangway-like structures leading to pilings or vessel mooring or berthing installations, which present a hazard of falling
more than 4 feet (1.22 m) or into the water.
Shipyard Industry 1915.73(d) - When employees are exposed to unguarded edges of decks, platforms, flats, and similar flat surfaces, more than 5
feet above a solid surface, the edges shall be guarded by adequate guardrails.
Steel Erection 1926.760(a)(1) - Each employee engaged in a steel erection activity who is on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or
edge more than 15 feet (4.6 m) above a lower level shall be protected from fall hazards by guardrail systems, safety net systems, personal fall arrest
systems, positioning device systems or fall restraint systems.
Incidents will be investigated. The investigation will look at the fall protection plan to see if any updates are needed to
keep the incident from happening again.
Equipment and services for prompt rescue of fallen workers must be available before elevated work begins. Local fire
departments may not have the means to perform safe and efficient rescue, so do not assume they are able to do so.
